To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the relationship between false belief understanding and social experience is apparent in elicited-response and non-elicited response tasks, and that this relationship is not specific to preschoolers but is apparent in adults and children across the lifespan.

(1) the capacity to represent others’ beliefs emerges in infancy; (2) social factors influence preschoolers’ performance, not by facilitating the emergence of false-belief understanding, but rather by affecting the processes that are necessary for the use of this capacity in elicited-response tests; and (3) this relationship between social factors (such as language, social class, and gender) and false-belief performance extends beyond preschoolers to adults.

social factors facilitate the performance of adults and preschoolers in elicited-response and non-elicited response paradigms, and that this facilitation is mediated by effects on attention, retrieval, and/or response production, but not by the emergence of the ability to represent beliefs.
In summary, our research is concerned with

understanding the nature of the relationship between social experience and false-belief ability, and we argue that this relationship is better understood in terms of the effects of social experience on the use of a capacity for belief representation that emerges in the 2nd half of the 1st postnatal year.
the relationship between social experience and children’s performance on false-belief tasks and, more generally, with the relationship between theory of mind and social cognition.
the relationship between social experience and the ability to represent false beliefs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
social factors are not necessary for false-belief understanding to emerge, and are instead necessary for the use of this understanding in a variety of tasks and contexts.
false-belief tasks are not a good way of measuring the ability to represent false beliefs.
the relationship between the social experience and the false-belief understanding is a complex one, which requires further research.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
false-belief tasks are more complex than they may seem at first glance.

social factors facilitate the application of a pre-existing ability to represent beliefs, and that the relationship between these factors and the use of this capacity emerges early and persists throughout the lifespan.
social experience facilitates the development and use of false-belief understanding.
The main takeaway from our work is that

false-belief tasks should be used to assess children’s ability to use their mentalizing capacity to represent beliefs in a particular context rather than to assess their general ability to represent beliefs.
social experience is not a cause of false-belief understanding, but rather a facilitator of its use.
the relationship between false-belief understanding and social experience is best explained by a mentalistic account that incorporates the role of non-cognitive factors.
